text.p: The Group of Seven (G7) is getting edgy about extreme moves in the currency markets but will probably hold off on any large-scale attempts at concerted intervention for now, analysts said on Tuesday.
Policymarkers in at least two G7 countries -- Germany and Britain -- are probably worried by how far sterling and the dollar have strengthened and how much the mark has fallen, they said.

Theo Waigel, Germany's finance minister, said on Tuesday strength in the dollar and sterling against the mark reflected an "over-reaction" by the market and that G7 members were in contact on forex developments.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the G7 were considering ways and means of stabilising currencies," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.
But he said a scattergun approach to intervention aimed at a few targeted currencies would probably be the first sign of protest.
The dollar has shot up against the mark in recent weeks, reaching a six-year high of 1.7995 marks on Monday. Since the start of the year it has climbed more than 25 pfennigs.
Sterling's rise is even more dramatic. Its 40-pfennig rally this year went into overdrive last week, culminating with a move above three marks.

Waigel's comments produced a swift but only temporary fall in both the dollar and sterling. The U.S. currency fell 3/4 of a pfennig to 1.7830 marks but by 0830 GMT was back at 1.7920/25. Sterling dropped nearly two pfennigs to 3.0045 marks before rebounding to 3.0225/35.
Edmonds said British authorities had already signaled they were not pleased by the extent of the pound's appreciation, while inflation-conscious Germany has reason to worry about the mark.
"We're already seeing some signs that price rises are starting to come through (in Germany) in the early stage of the producer price chain as a result of weakness in the mark," Edmonds said.
That, he said, would only be exacerbated by a dollar move above 1.80 marks.
Analysts said Japan is probably relatively happy with the yen, and that the U.S. is less concerned about currency levels than Britain and Germany.
"I don't think there will be any strong objections to G7 action but I don't see a unanimous decision in favour of strong action," Edmonds said.
Others said the G7 was unlikely to get involved at this stage because the mark's troubles were more to do with European matters than the global market.
"It's really a European issue and I don't think that it actually affects Japan or North America," said Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments.
Waigel, speaking at a news conference in Berlin, said: "We are interested in a strong deutschemark. I think what's happening at the moment is an overreaction of the markets."
He added that Germany had, as in the past, agreed cooperation within the G7. "We are in contact with our partners."
The expectation that EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) will result in a weaker euro than the mark has sparked widespread mark selling both this year and last.
"I agree with Waigel that the dollar strength against the mark has been overdone, but the mark has been driven by EMU factors," Howard said.
"You need to estimate what EMU risk premium has been factored into dollar/mark and we've estimated 20-25 pfennigs at current levels,"
There was market talk that the Bundesbank was checking mark prices on Tuesday but the German central bank declined to comment.
Analysts said any action by central banks would be behind-the-scenes smoothing, rather than the occasional "bells and whistles" approach the G7 has adopted in the past.

"The intervention threat is obvious given that the moves in the last couple of days have been very sharp and central banks tend to want to smooth volatility," said Eric Fishwick, analyst at Nikko Europe.
"(But) the markets are generally a lot more relaxed about the threat of forex intervention."
